title: Speech and slander (III.27–III.29)
hook: one sentence typed into a group chat about someone who isn't in it; Francis de Sales counts three wounds
tomorrow: why was an old apostle sitting there playing with a bird?

segments.voice: That was a week of Francis's shared virtues: humility that can say thank you, gentleness both ways, work without the hurry, a free heart, and true friends. Yesterday's line: true friends.

One sentence, typed into a group chat, about someone who isn't in it. A few laughing faces pop up underneath. It feels like nothing. Francis de Sales counts the wounded, and he gets three. The person talked about loses some of their good name. The people listening take the poison in. And the one who typed it harms their own soul. One stroke of the tongue, three wounds.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE, SOMEONE NOT THERE.` → `IT FEELS LIKE NOTHING.` → `THREE WOUNDS.`

segments.voice: His chapters on speech start wider. Our words show what's in the heart, Francis says, so he asks for speech that is clean, modest and respectful toward everyone. Then the step before slander: judging. He points to Christ's words in the Douay-Rheims: "Judge not, that you may not be judged." Rash judgment sees one act and pins a whole label on a person. One bad day doesn't make someone a bad person, and we rarely see the inside of another heart. Then slander itself, with its three wounds. He's especially wary of slander in disguise: a dig wrapped in a joke, or criticism that opens with a compliment. And the turn toward good. When someone is spoken ill of in front of you, excuse them if you fairly can, or gently change the subject. Speak of the absent the way you'd want to be spoken of when you're the one not in the room.
screen: `WORDS SHOW THE HEART.` · `JUDGE NOT.` · `A DIG WRAPPED IN A JOKE.` · `EXCUSE, OR CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` · then, large: `SPEAK WELL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who isn't here right now, maybe someone who's annoyed you lately. Through the sit, count three true, good things about them, one finger at a time. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Speech and slander. Words that show the heart, and Francis's three wounds when they're turned against someone absent.
Your line: speak well, most of all about the ones who aren't in the room. Two weeks, done.

howItsDone: Catholics count detraction and calumny, harming someone's good name, among sins against the truth, and name them in confession; the Catechism asks for interpreting others' words and deeds as favorably as possible.
